papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that quantizes subroutines of clustering and preprocessing algorithms with Grover-type search in a distance-oracle model and states query-count bounds, with no experiments.

assertions.value: The authors state that in their model the knowledge of the dataset comes only from a black box, or oracle, that can be queried for the distance between two points, that the complexity of an algorithm is measured in the number of queries to the oracle, and that they call this number of queries time.
quotes: In this model, our knowledge of the dataset comes uniquely from a black box (sometimes called oracle) that can be queried to learn the distance between two points.
Note that in this model, the complexity of an algorithm is measured in terms of the numbers of queries to the oracle
For simplicity, we shall henceforth refer to this number of queries as
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. 3.1 states the paper's model.
assertions.reader_inference: Every time bound in the paper is a query count to the distance oracle, not a gate count or wall-clock time.

assertions.value: The authors state that no assumptions are made about the distance except that it is non-negative and that a point has distance zero to itself, so the triangle inequality need not hold, and that they assume symmetry for simplicity.
quotes: No assumptions are made a priori concerning the properties of this distance except that it is non-negative and that Dist(xi, xi) = 0 for all i.
In particular, the triangle inequality need not hold and the distance may not be symmetric.
Throughout this paper, we shall nevertheless assume for simplicity that the distance function is symmetric
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. 3.1 states the setup.

assertions.value: The authors state that the assumption that a clustering problem is given as a black box is not realistic in practice, and they point to the quantum random access memory architectures of Giovannetti et al. (2008) as a way to build a circuit that plays the role of the oracle.
quotes: The assumption that a particular clustering problem is given as a black box is not realistic in practice
Giovannetti et al. (2008) have designed general quantum random access memory (QRAM) architectures
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. 3.1 states the limit on its own model.

assertions.value: The authors state that the oracle must be unitary and therefore reversible, and that this is not really a restriction because any classical irreversible circuit can be transformed into a reversible one for a reasonable cost, citing Bennett.

assertions.value: The authors state that building a quantum circuit or QRAM that stores every entry of the adjacency matrix would take at least order n squared time, because each entry of the n by n matrix must be read at least once, which is no better than using Prim's algorithm directly.
quotes: the construction of this circuit would require at least Ω(n2) time because one would need to read each entry of the n × n matrix at least once.
This is clearly not better than using directly Prim's algorithm.
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. 4 states the practical limit on the speed-up.
assertions.reader_inference: The n to the three halves bound holds only when the distance oracle itself costs no more than that to build.

quotes: Quantum mechanically, it is possible to use quant_find_max as a subroutine in this algorithm to find the two points that are the farthest apart in O(n) time.
The convergence proof of quant_find_max is similar to the analysis of Dürr and Høyer (1996) for their algorithm for finding the minimum of a function.

assertions.value: The paper defines the median of a set of points as a point whose sum of distances to all the other points is minimal, ties broken arbitrarily, and notes that in the multidimensional case the term medoid is sometimes used.
quotes: The median of a set of points D is one whose sum of distances with all the other points is minimal (ties are broken arbitrarily)
In the case of multidimensional points, the term medoid is sometimes used instead of the term median.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition 1.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the generic case, with no property of the distance to exploit, the naive classical computation of the median is the most efficient possible, and that a classical lower bound of order n squared follows from a scenario where all points are at equal distance except two closer points.
quotes: In the generic case, where there are no properties of the distance to be used or no structure within the ensemble of points that can be exploited, this naïve solution is the most efficient possible.
This results in a lower bound of Ω(n2) time.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper gives a short adversarial example, not a formal proof.

assertions.value: The paper states as Lemma 1 that, with high probability, algorithm quant_find_median finds the median among a set of n points in order n to the three halves time, from order square root of n applications of a circuit that sums distances in order n time.
quotes: Lemma 1 (Convergence of quant_find_median) With high probability, algorithm quant_find_median finds the median among a set of n points in O(n3/2) time.
This can be achieved in O(n) time by simply applying the black box described in Fig. 4 successively for each value of j
assertions.certainty_reason: The proof text is partly garbled in the text layer; the statement and the cost of the sum circuit are quoted.
assertions.reader_inference: The bound is the product of the order n cost of the sum circuit and the order square root of n cost of Durr and Hoyer minimum finding.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum algorithm of Nayak and Wu for approximating the median applies to numbers or colinear points, and does not apply when the only information is the distance between each pair of points.
quotes: When all the xi correspond simply to numbers, or more generally when all the points are colinear,
which corresponds to a situation for which the algorithm of Nayak and Wu does not apply.
assertions.certainty_reason: A scoping remark about cited work.

assertions.value: The authors state that a more efficient but approximate solution for the sum of distances was proposed by Brassard et al. (2011), and that they leave for further research the impact of approximate medians on the quality of the clustering.
quotes: A more efficient but approximate solution to this problem has recently been proposed by Brassard et al. (2011).
it is not obvious to determine how detrimental to the quality of the resulting clustering would this use of approximate medians be.
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. 3.2 states the open point.

assertions.value: The authors state that classically, with the graph given as an adjacency matrix, the clustering problem is solved by Prim's algorithm in order n squared time, and that this is optimal since all classical algorithms need order n squared time for a complete graph and an arbitrary metric.
quotes: Classically, when the graph is given as an adjacency matrix, this clustering problem can be solved directly by using Prim's algorithm (1957), which takes O(n2) time
This algorithm is optimal since all classical algorithms require Ω(n2) time in the case of a complete graph and an arbitrary metric.
assertions.certainty_reason: A classical result the paper cites and does not prove.

assertions.value: The authors state that the clustering obtained from a minimum spanning tree, by removing its k minus one heaviest edges, is precisely the one that maximizes the maximum-spacing criterion, citing Gower and Ross (1969).
quotes: it is easy to group the points into k clusters simply by removing the k − 1 heaviest edges of this tree.
The clustering based on the minimum spanning tree is precisely the one that maximizes this clustering criterion of maximum spacing (Gower and Ross 1969).
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited classical result.

assertions.value: The authors state that Theorem 3 implies a k-clustering with maximum spacing in order n to the three halves time, on condition that an efficient quantum circuit giving the distance between an arbitrary pair of points can be obtained in order n to the three halves time.
quotes: This theorem directly implies that it is possible to obtain a k-clustering with maximum spacing in Θ(n3/2) time, again on condition that an efficient quantum circuit to provide the distance between an arbitrary pair of points can be obtained in O(n3/2) time.
assertions.certainty_reason: Follows from a cited theorem; no separate proof.

assertions.value: The paper states as the fourth theorem that, with high probability, quantum divisive clustering of n points gains over the classical version, as measured by the ratio of classical to quantum times. The proof uses the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) for the balanced case, which is order n log n.
quotes: performs divisive clustering of a set of n points with a gain of
as measured by the ratio between the classical and quantum times.
the recurrence T (n) = 2T (n/2) + O(n), which is O(n log n)

assertions.reader_inference: From the proof, the gain is at least order n over log n; the unbalanced case gives a larger gain.

assertions.value: The authors state that for datapoints that are vectors in R^d of arbitrarily high dimension, finding the two farthest apart points requires order n squared comparisons in the general case, even for approximations, citing Finocchiaro and Pellegrini.

and this even in the case of approximations (Finocchiaro and Pellegrini 2002)

assertions.value: The authors state that optimizing the k-medians criterion is NP-hard for all k of at least two, even in the Euclidean case, so no polynomial-time algorithm is known even with a quantum computer, and that their quantum k-medians is a quantized heuristic and not an exact algorithm.
quotes: optimizing the k-medians criterion is NP-hard for all k 2 even in the Euclidean case (Papadimitriou 1981)

assertions.value: The authors state that the trivial distributed protocol, which gathers all the data at one site, has communication cost of order d times m bits, d the dimension and m the size of the smaller dataset, and that the trivial protocol on n points costs order d times n bits.
